p: Every morning, before the sun comes up, Fanta walks down to the river with a yellow bucket on her head.

The path is narrow and red. On both sides, there are tall grasses, mango trees and a few old baobabs with arms like giants. The birds are waking up. The air smells of wet earth and smoke from the kitchens. Behind her, the village of Sokala is still half asleep.

Fanta is twelve years old. She is small for her age, with big eyes, short hair and a gap between her two front teeth. She lives with her mother, her father, her little brother Bakary and her grandmother, Mama Ténin, in a house with three rooms and a big courtyard.

Her father, Drissa, is a fisherman. Every day, he goes out on the river in his pirogue, a long wooden boat, with his net. Her mother, Salimata, grows vegetables near the water and sells them at the market. Bakary is six, and he is always hungry, always dirty and always happy.

Sokala is a small village on the bank of the Comoé, the longest river in Côte d'Ivoire. Everything in Sokala comes from the river: the water to drink, the water to cook, the water to wash, the fish, the vegetables, the cool wind in the afternoon. The river is the heart of the village.
But for Fanta, the river is something more.
The river is her friend.
At the bottom of the path, there is a flat rock next to the water. Fanta puts down her bucket. She looks around. Nobody is there. Good.
She sits on the rock, and she puts her right hand in the water. It is cool and soft, like silk.
She closes her eyes. And she waits.
*Hello, little one.*
The voice comes from everywhere and nowhere. It is old and soft, like a grandmother singing to a baby. It is not in her ears. It is inside her, in her chest, in her head, in her hand.
"Good morning, River," whispers Fanta. "Did you sleep well?"
*Rivers don't sleep, little one. We run all night. But I had beautiful dreams. A family of hippos passed by. The mother was very fat and very proud.*
Fanta laughs.
It started when she was five years old. One day, she followed her mother to the river. She put her little hand in the water to catch a fish, and she heard the voice for the first time.
*Hello, little one.*
She ran home, very excited. "Maman! Maman! The river said hello to me!"
Her mother laughed. "Rivers don't talk, Fanta. Go and get water, and stop dreaming."
Her friends laughed too. "Fanta talks to the river! Fanta talks to fish!" For weeks, the other children followed her and made fish faces. Fanta cried every night.
So Fanta stopped telling people. She learned to keep her secret. Now, nobody knows. Not her mother, not her father, not even her best friend, Kadi.
But every morning, she comes to the flat rock. And every morning, the river talks to her.
"I have to go," says Fanta. "I have school today. Monsieur Yéo is giving us a test on the planets."
*Then go, little one. And remember what I always tell you.*
Fanta smiles. She knows the words by heart.
"Be kind to me," she says, "and I will be kind to you."
*Exactly.*

She fills her yellow bucket with water. She puts it on her head and walks back up the red path. The sun is rising now, big and orange, behind the baobabs. The water in her bucket moves a little, and it shines like gold.
Behind her, the river runs, quiet and strong, as it has run for thousands of years.
Fanta doesn't know it yet. But very soon, her old friend will need her help.
The river knows a lot of stories. It is very old, older than the village, older than the forest, older than the oldest grandmother.
Every morning, it tells Fanta a new one.

It tells her about the fish: the capitaine, big and lazy, who sleeps in the deep water; the little silver fish who swim together like a cloud; the strange fish with whiskers like an old man, who eats everything.

It tells her about Old Bassa, the crocodile. *He is a hundred years old,* says the river. *He is grumpy, and he has only twelve teeth left. But he is my friend. Never be afraid of him, little one. He knows you.*

It tells her about the old kings who lived on its banks a long time ago, with their gold, their drums and their elephants. It tells her about the people who crossed it in pirogues to escape wars, about the women who sang while they washed clothes, about the lovers who met in secret under the trees.
*Everybody comes to me,* says the river. *Happy people, sad people, thirsty people. I give them water. I listen to them. I keep their secrets.*
"Do you keep my secret too?" asks Fanta.
*Always, little one. Always.*
At school, Fanta is a good student. Her teacher, Monsieur Yéo, is a young man from Korhogo with round glasses and a big laugh. He loves science.
One day, he draws a map of Côte d'Ivoire on the blackboard. He draws four long blue lines.

"These are the four big rivers of our country," he says. "The Cavally, the Sassandra, the Bandama and the Comoé. Our river, the Comoé, is the longest. It starts in Burkina Faso and it goes all the way to the sea, near Grand-Bassam. More than one thousand kilometres!"
Fanta raises her hand. "Monsieur, what happens to a river when people are not kind to it?"

Monsieur Yéo looks at her with interest. "That's a very good question, Fanta. When people throw rubbish in a river, or chemicals from factories, the water becomes dirty. The fish die. People who drink the water get sick. And when people take too much water from a river, for farms or for cities, the river becomes small. Sometimes, it disappears completely."
"Disappears?" Fanta's heart jumps.
"Yes. There are rivers in the world that don't reach the sea anymore. People killed them."
The other children write in their notebooks. But Fanta doesn't write. She looks out of the window, towards the river, and she feels cold inside.
After school, Fanta walks home with Kadi. Kadi is her best friend. She is tall and loud, with long braids and a laugh you can hear from the other side of the village. She wants to be a famous singer.
"Monsieur Yéo is so boring with his rivers," says Kadi. "Who cares about rivers? Rivers are just... water."
Fanta stops walking. "Rivers are not just water, Kadi."
"Then what are they?"
Fanta wants to tell her. She wants to tell her about the voice, the stories, Old Bassa and the hippos. But she remembers the fish faces, the laughing, the crying at night.
"Nothing," she says. "Forget it."
Kadi looks at her strangely. Then she shrugs and starts to sing a song from the radio.
That evening, at dinner, Fanta's father is quiet. He eats his attiéké and fish slowly.
"What's wrong, Drissa?" asks Fanta's mother.
"The fish," he says. "There are fewer fish this year. Every week, I catch less. Today, I caught only five. Five fish, after eight hours on the river."
"It's the season," says Salimata. "It will get better."
But Mama Ténin, Fanta's grandmother, doesn't say anything. She looks at Fanta. And Fanta has the strange feeling that her grandmother knows something.
That year, the rains don't come.

Usually, in Sokala, the rainy season starts in April. Big grey clouds come from the south, the sky becomes dark, and then — boom! — the rain falls, heavy and warm, for hours. The earth drinks. The maize grows. Everybody is happy.
But this year, April passes, and the sky stays blue. May passes, and the sky stays blue. In June, there is one small storm, for ten minutes. Then nothing.

The sun burns the fields. The leaves of the maize become yellow, then brown. The ground cracks like an old plate. The goats and the cows are thin and thirsty. The farmers look at the sky every morning and shake their heads.
And the river becomes smaller.
Every morning, Fanta walks a little further to find the water. The flat rock, her rock, is now far from the river. There is a long beach of dry mud between the rock and the water. The mud smells bad.
And every morning, the river's voice is weaker.
*Hello... little one.*
"River! Are you OK?"
*I am tired, little one. Very tired.*
"Is it because there is no rain?"
The river is silent for a long time. Then it says: *The rain is late, yes. But it is not only the rain. There is something else. Something new.*
"What?"
*Far, far upstream, men are taking my water. A lot of water. More every month. And they put something in me. Something black and bitter. It burns. It makes the fish sick.*
Fanta feels cold, even in the hot sun. "Who? Which men?"
*I don't know their names. They came with big machines. They built something across me. A wall. I can feel it, like a hand around my neck.*
"I'll tell someone! I'll tell the chief! I'll tell everybody!"
*They won't believe you, little one.*
"They have to believe me!"
The next week, the water becomes strange. It is not clear anymore. It is a little green, and sometimes, on the surface, there are shiny colours, like a rainbow. Like oil.
Salimata, Fanta's mother, comes home from her garden with a worried face. "The tomatoes are dying. The water burns their roots."
Fanta's father comes home with three fish. Two of them have strange white spots on their skin. He throws them away. "We can't eat these," he says.
And then, children in the village start to get sick.

First, it is Kadi's little sister, Mimi. She has a fever and a terrible pain in her stomach. Then two boys from the other side of the village. Then a baby. The nurse from the health centre in the next town comes on her motorbike. She looks at the children. She looks at the water.
"Don't drink the river water," she says. "Boil it first. Always. Or better, don't drink it at all."
"But we have no other water," says the chief. "The well is dry since March."
The nurse doesn't answer. She gives medicine to the children, gets on her motorbike, and leaves in a cloud of red dust.

That night, Fanta can't sleep. She lies on her mat and listens to the sounds of the night: the insects, a dog, her little brother breathing next to her. And in her head, she hears the river's weak, tired voice.
*They won't believe you, little one.*
"They have to," she whispers in the dark. "They have to."
Tomorrow, she decides, she will tell the chief everything.

The chief of Sokala is called Nanan Koné. He is a very old man with a white beard and a long stick with a silver lion on top. Every afternoon, he sits under the big tree in the middle of the village, with the old men, and they talk about the problems of the village.
Today, the big problem is the water.
"The river is sick," says one old man. "My grandfather never saw the river so small."
"It's the dry season," says another. "It's God's will. We must pray for rain."
"We must dig a new well," says a third. "Deeper."
"With what money?" says Nanan Koné.
Nobody answers.

That's when Fanta arrives. She is shaking, but she walks straight to the chief and stands in front of him. Children never interrupt the old men under the big tree. Never. Everybody stops talking and looks at her.
"Nanan," she says. Her voice is small. She takes a deep breath and says it again, louder. "Nanan Koné. I know why the river is sick."
The chief looks at her with surprise. "You are Drissa's daughter. Fanta."
"Yes, Nanan."
"Speak, my child. Why is the river sick?"
"Men are taking its water. Far upstream. They built a wall across it. And they put something black and bitter in the water. That's why the fish are sick. That's why the children are sick."
The old men look at each other.
"And how do you know this, little girl?" asks the chief. "Did you go upstream?"
Fanta hesitates. Then she decides to tell the truth.
"The river told me."
For a second, there is silence. Then one old man starts to laugh. Then another. Then all of them. They laugh so much that one of them almost falls off his chair.
"The river told her!" says one. "Next week, the goats will tell us the price of rice!"
"Maybe the fish can be our new chief!"
Fanta's face is hot. Her eyes are full of tears. But she doesn't move.
"It's true!" she says. "The river talks to me! Every morning! Since I was five!"

The laughing becomes louder. Some women and children come to see what is happening. Somebody says, "Fanta talks to fish!" and the children start to make fish faces, like before, like when she was five.
Nanan Koné raises his hand, and everybody becomes quiet. He looks at Fanta kindly, but sadly.

"My child," he says. "I believe that you love the river. That is a good thing. But it is the dry season. Rivers are always small in the dry season. And rivers do not talk. Go home now. Help your mother."
Fanta runs. She runs past the laughing children, past the houses, past the market, all the way to her house. She runs into her room, throws herself on her mat, and cries.
She cries for a long time.
Later, Kadi comes. She sits on the floor next to Fanta and doesn't say anything for a while.
"Is it true?" asks Kadi finally. "Does the river really talk to you?"
Fanta looks at her through her tears. "You're going to laugh too."
"I'm not laughing," says Kadi. And she isn't. Her face is serious. "My little sister is sick, Fanta. Mimi is very sick. If you know something, I want to know too."
So Fanta tells her. Everything. The voice, the stories, Old Bassa, the hippos, the wall, the black water.
Kadi listens without a word. When Fanta finishes, Kadi is quiet for a long time.
"I don't know if I believe you," she says finally. "But I believe that you believe it. And you never lie. So... what do we do?"
Fanta doesn't know.
But in the doorway, someone is watching them. An old woman with a blue headscarf and a face full of wrinkles.
It is Mama Ténin. And she is not laughing either.
That night, when everybody is asleep, Mama Ténin wakes Fanta up.
"Come," she whispers. "Don't make noise."

Fanta follows her grandmother across the dark courtyard, to the small round hut where Mama Ténin sleeps. Inside, there is a little oil lamp, a mat, an old wooden box, and the smell of shea butter and old cloth.
Mama Ténin sits down slowly. Her knees are old and they hurt. She points to the mat. "Sit."
Fanta sits.
For a long moment, the old woman looks at her granddaughter in the yellow light of the lamp.
"When I was a girl," she says finally, "I heard the river too."
Fanta's mouth falls open.

"Every morning, like you. On a flat rock, like you. It called me *little one*, like you. And it told me stories. About the hippos. About the old kings. About Old Bassa, when he was young and had all his teeth."
"Grandmother! Why didn't you tell me?"

"Because I wasn't sure. You never said anything. And because..." She sighs. "Because people laugh. People are afraid of what they don't understand. When I was young, I told my village. They called me a witch. My own mother was ashamed of me. So I stopped talking about it. And after many years, I stopped hearing it too."
"You stopped hearing the river?"

"When you stop listening, the river stops talking. That is how it is." She smiles sadly. "But today, under the big tree, I saw you stand in front of all those old men. Alone. And you told the truth, even when they laughed. I was never so brave, Fanta. Never."

"It is a gift in our family," Mama Ténin continues. "My grandmother had it. Her grandmother had it. It goes from grandmother to granddaughter, and it jumps over the mothers. Only girls have it. And only girls with a clean heart."
"Why us?"
"Who knows? Maybe a long, long time ago, one of our grandmothers did something kind for the river. Maybe she saved it, like you want to save it now. And the river never forgot."

Then the old woman opens the wooden box. Inside, wrapped in a piece of old indigo cloth, there is a small stone. It is smooth and round, the size of an egg, and it is blue — a deep, clear blue, like the sky at seven o'clock in the evening.
"This stone comes from the bottom of the river," says Mama Ténin. "From the deepest place, where no fisherman can go. My grandmother gave it to me. Now I give it to you."
She puts it in Fanta's hand. It is cold, then warm. It seems to move a little, like something alive.
"If you hold this stone and you call the river, it can show you what it sees. Not only here. Everywhere. All along its body, from Burkina Faso to the sea."
Fanta holds the stone tightly. She closes her eyes.
"River," she whispers. "Show me. Please. Show me what is making you sick."
At first, nothing. Only darkness and the sound of her own heart.

Then, slowly, pictures come. As if she is a fish, swimming very fast against the current. Past Sokala. Past other villages, other fishermen. Past forests and fields and a bridge. Two days, three days of water.
And then, she sees it.

A big grey wall of concrete across the river. Behind the wall, a lake of still, dark water. Huge pipes, as big as houses, sucking the water out. Fields of sugar cane, green and endless, as far as she can see. And a factory, with tall chimneys and black smoke. Next to the factory, hidden behind some trees, a small pipe pours a thick, black liquid into the river.
Fanta opens her eyes. She is breathing very fast.
"A wall," she says. "A factory. Sugar cane. And a black pipe, hidden in the trees."
Mama Ténin nods slowly. "Then we know what to do."
"What?"
The old woman smiles. Her eyes shine in the lamplight like a young girl's.
"We go there."
"You are both crazy," says Fanta's father.
It is early in the morning. In the courtyard, Mama Ténin has a small bag ready, and Fanta has her school backpack with some clothes, bread and a bottle of boiled water.
"An old woman of seventy-four and a girl of twelve, walking for days, to a factory, because a river told them?" Drissa shakes his head. "No. No, no, no."

"I am not asking for permission, my son," says Mama Ténin calmly. "I am telling you. Children are sick. The fish are dying. Your tomatoes are dying. And the men under the big tree only talk and pray. Someone must do something."
Salimata, Fanta's mother, looks at her daughter for a long time. "Fanta," she says. "Is it true? The river... really?"
Fanta looks at her mother. "Yes, Maman. It's true. Since I was five."
Salimata closes her eyes. Then she opens them, and she takes a few coins from her pagne and puts them in Fanta's hand.
"For food," she says. "And come back."
Drissa looks at his wife, at his mother, at his daughter. Then he sighs a very long sigh.
"I'm not letting you walk," he says. "I'll take you in the pirogue."
So they leave Sokala in Drissa's long wooden pirogue: Drissa at the back with his paddle, Mama Ténin in the middle on a folded pagne, and Fanta at the front, with the blue stone in her pocket.
At the last moment, someone runs down the path to the river, shouting. It's Kadi, with a plastic bag in her hand.
"Wait! I'm coming too!"
"Kadi! Your mother—"
"My mother said yes. Mimi is still sick. I want to do something." She jumps into the pirogue, which moves dangerously. "Also, I brought peanuts."

Going upstream is hard. The water is low, so in many places, the pirogue touches the bottom, and they have to get out and push. The sun is terrible. Drissa's arms are tired after a few hours. Kadi helps him with a second paddle, and she sings to give him strength. Her voice is loud and beautiful, and it goes far over the water.
Every hour, Fanta puts her hand in the river.
"Courage, River. We're coming."
*I know, little one. I can feel you. Your little boat tickles.*

They pass other villages. Everywhere, it is the same: low water, dead fish, worried faces. In one village, an old fisherman tells them, "Since the big farm opened, two years ago, the river is dying. But they are powerful people. Rich people. What can we do?"
At night, they sleep on a sandbank, under the stars. Drissa makes a small fire. Mama Ténin tells stories from her youth. Kadi falls asleep in the middle of a song.
Fanta can't sleep. She sits at the edge of the water with her hand in the river.
Suddenly, two yellow eyes appear in the dark water, very close. A long, grey shape. A crocodile. A very old crocodile, with only twelve teeth.
Fanta doesn't move. She doesn't scream.
"Old Bassa?" she whispers.

The crocodile looks at her for a long moment. Then it turns slowly and swims around the sandbank, once, twice, three times, like a guard. And then it stays in the water, near the pirogue, all night long.
*He came to protect you,* says the river softly. *I told you. He knows you.*
On the morning of the third day, they see a strange thing on the horizon. A big grey line across the river. Above it, tall chimneys and a cloud of dark smoke.
The wall. The factory.
Kadi stops singing. Drissa stops paddling. Mama Ténin takes Fanta's hand.
"It's exactly like in my vision," whispers Fanta.
Her father looks at her. And for the first time, there is no doubt in his eyes. Only fear, and a kind of respect.
"Then let's go and see these rich, powerful people," he says.

The factory is enormous. Fanta has never seen a building so big. It is bigger than the whole village of Sokala. There are metal towers, long pipes, trucks full of sugar cane, and a terrible noise of machines that never stops. The air smells sweet and burnt at the same time, like caramel left too long on the fire.
Around the factory, there is a tall fence with barbed wire. And in the fence, there is a big gate, with a sign:
**SUCRE DU NORD — PRIVATE PROPERTY — NO ENTRY**
Next to the gate, in a small house, there is a guard in a blue uniform. He is young, with a big belly and a radio playing music.
"Good morning," says Mama Ténin politely. "We want to see the director, please."
The guard looks at them: an old woman, a fisherman, two dusty girls. He laughs.
"The director? You want to see the director? Do you have an appointment?"
"No."
"Then no." He turns up the music on his radio. "Go home, Mama."
They don't go home.

Mama Ténin sits down on a rock in front of the gate. Drissa sits next to her. Kadi sits next to Drissa. And Fanta sits in front of all of them, right in front of the gate, with her back very straight.
"We are waiting for the director," says Mama Ténin to the guard. "We have time."
The guard shrugs. "Wait all you want. She doesn't come out this way."
The hours pass. The sun is hot. Trucks go in and out, and the drivers look at the strange group in front of the gate. Some laugh. Some honk their horns. One driver throws them a bottle of water.

At noon, Kadi starts to sing. Not a radio song. An old song from Sokala, about the river. Mama Ténin knows it, and she sings too. Then Drissa. Then Fanta. Their voices are not very loud against the noise of the machines, but they don't stop.

Workers come out of the factory for their lunch break. They hear the singing. Some of them stop to listen. One of them, an old worker with grey hair, starts to sing too. He knows the song. He is from a village on the river too.
"What are you doing here?" he asks Drissa.
Drissa tells him. The low water. The dead fish. The sick children.

The old worker looks behind him, at the factory, and then he speaks in a low voice. "You should talk to the engineer. Mademoiselle Esther. She's new. She's young. She asks a lot of questions. The bosses don't like her very much." He smiles. "That means she's a good person."

In the afternoon, a white car comes out of the gate. It stops. A young woman gets out. She is about thirty, with short hair, glasses, a white helmet and boots covered in mud. She has a tablet in her hand.
"What's happening here?" she asks the guard. "Why are these people sitting in front of the gate?"
"They want to see the director, Mademoiselle Esther. I told them no."
The young woman looks at Fanta. Fanta stands up.
"Good afternoon, Madame. My name is Fanta Ouattara. I come from Sokala. It's a village on the river. Three days down the river, by pirogue."
"Three days? In a pirogue?" Esther looks at the old woman, the fisherman, the other girl. "You came all this way... why?"
Fanta takes a deep breath. She thinks about the chief, the old men, the laughing. She thinks about Mimi, sick in her bed. She thinks about the river's weak, tired voice.
And she tells the truth. All of it. Even the part about the voice.
Esther doesn't laugh.
But she doesn't believe it either. Fanta can see it in her eyes. Esther is a scientist. Scientists don't believe in talking rivers.

"Listen," says Esther gently. "I can see that your village has a real problem. Low water, sick fish, sick children. That's serious. But the factory respects all the rules. We take only the water we are allowed to take. And we clean our waste water before it goes back to the river. I check it myself, every week."
"Not all of it," says Fanta.
"What do you mean?"
"There is another pipe. A small black one. It's hidden in the trees, behind the factory, near a big kapok tree. It pours black water into the river. At night, mostly."
Esther stops smiling.
"There is no pipe like that," she says slowly. "I know every pipe in this factory. I have the plans."
"Then it's not on your plans," says Fanta. "But it's there. The river showed me."
Esther looks at Fanta for a long time. Then she looks at her tablet. Then at the factory. Then at Fanta again.
"Get in the car," she says. "All of you."
The guard opens his mouth. "Mademoiselle, they are not allowed—"
"They are with me," says Esther. "Open the gate."

The white car drives along the fence, behind the factory, on a dirt road. They pass huge piles of sugar cane, trucks, workers. Then the road ends, and there are only trees, and the sound of the river.
Esther stops the car. "The big kapok tree. Where?"
Fanta closes her eyes. She holds the blue stone in her pocket. She can hear the river, very close.
*Left, little one. Go left. Follow my voice.*
"This way," says Fanta.
They walk through the trees. The ground is wet and the smell is terrible, like rotten eggs and burnt oil. Kadi puts her hand over her nose. Mama Ténin walks slowly, with Drissa holding her arm.
And then they see it.

A giant kapok tree, with roots like walls. And between the roots, half hidden by leaves and branches, a black pipe comes out of the ground. From the end of the pipe, a thick, dark liquid is running slowly into the river. Around it, the water is black. On the bank, there are dead fish. Many dead fish.
Esther doesn't say anything. She kneels next to the pipe. She takes a small bottle out of her bag and fills it with the black liquid. Her hands are shaking.

"This isn't on any plan," she says quietly. "This pipe goes directly from the old cleaning tanks to the river. Somebody built it in secret. So they don't have to clean the waste water. Cleaning costs a lot of money."
She stands up. Her face is pale and angry.
"Somebody is saving money," she says, "and your children are paying for it."
Then she turns to Fanta, and she looks at her very strangely.
"How did you know?" she asks. "Really. Nobody knows about this pipe. I've worked here for six months, and I didn't know. How did a twelve-year-old girl from a village three days away know?"
Fanta shrugs. "I told you, Madame. The river told me."
Esther opens her mouth. Closes it. Opens it again.
"I'm a scientist," she says finally. "I don't believe in talking rivers."
"That's OK," says Mama Ténin with a little smile. "The river believes in you."
Esther takes photos of the pipe with her tablet. Many photos. She records a video. She marks the place on a map. Then she takes them back to the car and drives straight to the main building.
"Wait here," she says.
She goes inside. Through the big windows, they can see her walking fast down a long corridor, her muddy boots leaving marks on the clean white floor.

Twenty minutes later, she comes back. With her is a woman of about fifty, in an elegant green dress, with grey hair in a neat bun and a serious face. On her jacket, there is a badge: *Mme A. DIABATÉ — Director.*
The director looks at the little group: the old woman, the fisherman, the two dusty girls.

"Mademoiselle Esther showed me the photos," she says. "And the sample. I didn't know about this pipe. I swear to you, I didn't know." She is silent for a moment. "But that is not an excuse. This is my factory. It is my responsibility."
She turns to Fanta.
"Esther tells me you came three days by pirogue. To tell us this."
"Yes, Madame."
"And she tells me that a river told you about the pipe."
Fanta lifts her chin. "Yes, Madame."
The director looks at her for a long moment. Then, to everybody's surprise, she smiles a little.
"My grandmother was from a village on the Bandama," she says. "When I was a child, she told me that the river spoke to the women of her family." She shakes her head. "I thought it was just a story."

That evening, Madame Diabaté invites them to eat in the factory restaurant. Fanta has never seen so much food in one place: rice, chicken, alloco, salad, fruit juice in big glass jugs. Kadi eats three plates. Drissa eats quietly, still a little afraid of all the white tables and the air conditioning.
After dinner, the director sits down with them. Esther is there too, with her tablet.

"I made some phone calls this afternoon," says Madame Diabaté. "The man who built the secret pipe is the old production manager. He left the company last month. The police are looking for him now. The pipe will be closed tonight. Tonight, not tomorrow."
"Thank you," says Mama Ténin.
"Don't thank me yet. That's not enough." The director looks at Esther. "Tell them."

Esther shows them a graph on her tablet. "The pipe is not the only problem. The wall — the dam — takes too much water for the sugar cane. Much more than the rules allow. Some people here changed the numbers in the reports. When there is a lot of rain, it's not a big problem. But this year, with no rain..." She looks at Fanta. "We are taking the river's water, and we are leaving nothing for the villages downstream."
"Like a hand around its neck," says Fanta quietly.
Esther looks at her. "Yes. Exactly like that."
The director takes a pen and a notebook. She writes as she speaks.

"So here is my promise. One: from tomorrow morning, we open the gates of the dam. Not completely — the cane needs water too — but enough for the river to live. Every day, we will measure the water downstream, and Esther will check it herself."
"Two: we will clean all our waste water. All of it. Every drop. And we will test the river every week, in every village from here to Sokala. The results will be public."
"Three: the factory will pay for a new well in Sokala. A deep well, with a pump. And for the medicine of all the sick children in the villages downstream."
She puts down her pen.
"And four," she says, looking at Fanta. "I want to come to Sokala. I want to see your village, and your river, with my own eyes. And I want to apologise to your people. In person."
Fanta looks at Mama Ténin. Mama Ténin looks at Drissa. Drissa, who is a quiet man, does something surprising. He stands up and takes the director's hand in both of his.
"Madame," he says. "In my village, we say that a promise is like a pirogue. It's easy to build. It's hard to paddle all the way."
Madame Diabaté nods seriously. "Then I will paddle," she says.
That night, they sleep in a small house for visitors at the factory. Real beds, with sheets. Kadi falls asleep in two seconds.
But Fanta goes out. She walks down to the river in the moonlight, behind the factory, to a place where the water is still clean. She sits on a rock and puts her hand in the water.
"River? Can you hear me?"
For a moment, there is nothing. Then, very weakly:
*I hear you, little one.*
"They're going to close the black pipe. Tonight. And tomorrow, they open the wall. A little. Every day."
Silence. Then the river says something it has never said before.
*Thank you.*
Fanta feels tears on her cheeks. "You're welcome."
*Do you know why I talk to your family, little one? I never told your grandmother. I never told her grandmother.*
"Why?"

*A long time ago, many hundreds of years ago, there was a terrible dry season. Worse than this one. I was almost dead. And a girl from your family — she was twelve years old, like you — carried water from a far spring, every day, for weeks, and poured it into me. Bucket after bucket. Alone. Everybody laughed at her. But she didn't stop. And I lived.*
The river's voice is soft.

*I never forgot her. And I never forgot her children, and her children's children. You are her granddaughter, little one, from very far away. Be kind to me, and I will be kind to you. That is our promise. Older than any wall.*
Fanta sits by the water until the moon goes down.
They go home with the current, so the trip is faster: only two days. Every hour, Fanta puts her hand in the water, and every hour, the river's voice is a little stronger.
*Do you feel it, little one? Do you feel it? The wall is open. I am running again!*

And she can see it. The water is higher. The mud beaches are smaller. The water is clear again. On the second day, a group of silver fish swims next to the pirogue, like a cloud, like in the river's stories. Kadi screams with joy. Drissa laughs, a big laugh, the first one in months.
On the second night, Old Bassa swims next to them for a long time. Then he turns and disappears into the dark water.
"Goodbye, Old Bassa," whispers Fanta. "Thank you."
When they arrive in Sokala, the whole village is waiting on the bank. Somebody saw the pirogue from far away, and the news ran faster than the river.

Fanta's mother runs into the water up to her knees and holds Fanta so tight that she can't breathe. Bakary jumps on his father's back. Kadi's mother cries and laughs. And little Mimi is there too, still thin, but standing, smiling, in her mother's arms.

"The medicine arrived yesterday," says the nurse, who is there with her motorbike. "A truck came from a factory in the north. With medicine for all the children. And clean water in big bottles. Nobody knows why."
Fanta and Mama Ténin look at each other and smile.
One week later, a white car comes to Sokala. Then another one. Then a big truck with machines.

Madame Diabaté gets out of the first car, in her green dress, with Esther in her muddy boots. The whole village comes to see. Nanan Koné, the chief, receives them under the big tree, with all the old men.
The director talks to the village for a long time. She explains about the dam, the black pipe, the reports with false numbers. She apologises. She promises. She shows the plans for the new well.
The old men listen in silence. When she finishes, Nanan Koné asks her one question.
"Madame. How did you find the secret pipe?"
Madame Diabaté turns around. She points at Fanta, who is standing at the back with Kadi.
"She found it," she says. "A daughter of your village, Fanta Ouattara. She came three days by pirogue to tell us. Without her, the pipe would still be there."
Everybody turns to look at Fanta. The old men. The women. The children who made fish faces. Fanta wants to disappear into the ground.

Nanan Koné stands up slowly, with his stick. He walks across the square to Fanta. He stops in front of her. And then, in front of the whole village, the old chief does something no chief of Sokala has ever done.
He bows his head to a twelve-year-old girl.

"Fanta," he says. "I laughed at you. We all laughed at you. We were wrong. Forgive an old man." He puts his hand on her head. "From today, you are the guardian of the river. When the river speaks, Sokala will listen."
And this time, nobody laughs.
The well is finished in three weeks. It is deep, and the water is cold and clean.
And two days after the well is finished, the rain finally comes.

It comes at night, with thunder and lightning. Heavy, warm, wonderful rain. It falls on the dry fields, on the cracked earth, on the roofs, on the river. Fanta wakes up and runs outside. Kadi is already there, dancing in the courtyard in her nightdress. Bakary runs out, then her mother, then her father. Even Mama Ténin comes out of her hut, and lifts her face to the sky, and lets the rain wash it.
They dance in the mud until morning.

Months later, the maize is tall and green. The fish are back. Drissa catches so many that he has to sell some in the next town. Salimata's tomatoes are red and fat. Monsieur Yéo starts a club at school called *The Friends of the River*. Thirty children join. Kadi writes a song about the river, and she sings it on the radio in Abengourou.
Esther comes to Sokala every month to test the water. Every time, she brings books for Fanta. Books about rivers, about water, about engineers.
"Maybe one day," she says, "you can come and work with me. The world needs people who listen to rivers. Even if they're scientists."
"Especially if they're scientists," says Fanta.

And every morning, before the sun comes up, Fanta still walks down the red path with her yellow bucket on her head. She still sits on the flat rock — which is next to the water again. She still puts her hand in the river.
*Hello, little one,* says the river. Its voice is strong and young again, full of laughter.
"Hello, old friend," says Fanta.
And then, very softly, so that nobody else can hear, she adds the words that her family has kept for hundreds of years:
"Be kind to me, and I will be kind to you."
*Always,* sings the river. *Always.*
**THE END**

title: The Girl Who Talked to the River
author: Léxi
desc: Fanta, 12 ans, entend la voix du fleuve Comoé. Quand le fleuve tombe malade, personne ne la croit… Avec sa grand-mère, elle remonte le fleuve en pirogue pour le sauver. Roman complet.
